newsitem.title: UK: Aluminium stocks continue slide, zinc stocks rise.
newsitem.headline: Aluminium stocks continue slide, zinc stocks rise.

text.p: The relentless decline in London Metal Exchange (LME) aluminium inventories, which fell by a net 17,500 tonnes over the past week, has failed to halt the steady slide in futures prices, traders said.

Elsewhere, the pace of declines in copper slowed but took the supply and demand balance to critical levels, while zinc stock believed to be of Chinese origin started to flow into LME Singapore warehouses.
LME aluminium stocks have declined by 228,225 tonnes, or 24.40 percent, since the beginning of 1997 to a current level of 706,850 tonnes.
But traders said the material moving out of LME warehouses was not going to end-users but was being used in financing operations.
"The metal is not going to consumers, it is just being tied up in deals. That's why the price has not moved higher," one trader said.
On Thursday the LME said it was making further changes to stock transparency, following the review of the market by the UK regulator, the Securities and Investments Board (SIB).
From October 1 stocks of formerly warranted metal held in LME warehouses pending movement out of the facility will be reported separately as part of the daily stock reporting process.

"Despite the impressive inventory reduction the market remains suspicious of the scale and influence of unreported stock," Flemings Global Mining said in a preview of its 1997 review of metal price forecasts to 2000.
Flemings said inventories would have to continue to fall to make up a 1997 supply shortfall that it estimated at 420,000 tonnes.
"Inventories which have already fallen 400,000 since the end of 1996 will have to continue to fall to feed the deficit," Flemings said.
Copper stocks had a net fall of 6,975 tonnes over the week. Total stocks now stand at 125,650 tonnes, up 9,975 tonnes since the start of the year.
Traders said the pace of declines in copper stocks, which have been falling since mid-May, looked to be slowing as the market entered the traditional slow summer period.
Martin Squires of Rudolf Wolff said conditions were slack in the physical copper market, but the very low level of stocks had left the market susceptible to prices spikes.
Squires believed China could be a major influence on copper's next move. "The market continues to discuss the potential for increased Chinese purchases this year," he said.
"However we feel that with the high copper price the Chinese are likely to be keen sellers rather than buyers assuming they have available material.".
Squires said stock movements needed to be watched carefully in the coming weeks for any indication of a turnaround in market fundamentals.
Zinc inventories recorded a net rise of 3,475 tonnes for the week as material seeped into Singapore warehouses.
Several traders suggested that the material was of Chinese origin, and they were expecting more shipments to arrive over the coming weeks.
Nickel stocks fell a net 1,068 tonnes on reports that the physical market had picked up on the back of the Inco and Norilsk disruptions.
